newsitem.title: UK: Britain urges N.Irish sides to avert parade strife.
newsitem.headline: Britain urges N.Irish sides to avert parade strife.

text.p: Britain on Thursday urged Northern Ireland's feuding Protestants and Catholics to seek agreement to avert violence during the British-ruled province's volatile annual parade season.
But the pro-British Protestant marching group, the Orange Order, reacted coolly to a compromise initiative proposed by rival Unionist and Nationalist newspapers.

Northern Ireland Secretary Mo Mowlam said the government would not tolerate a repeat of violence which overshadowed parades last summer and did not rule out drafting in extra police from mainland Britain.
"The rule of law must be upheld," she said in a BBC interview.
But she stressed she wanted to encourage mediation and was not prepared to give up hope yet .

"If we fall into that kind of talk early on, we are admitting defeat. I am not prepared to do that because I think there is rationality and common sense in Northern Ireland and that people -- the vast majority -- do not want a repeat of last year."
Two newspapers on opposite sides of Northern Ireland's sectarian divide called for compromise over a disputed parade scheduled in the town of Portadown on July 6.

In "a historic joint appeal", the News Letter, which is read mainly by pro-British Protestants, and the Irish News, bought chiefly by Catholics, said last summer's upheaval "was a disaster for all the people of Northern Ireland".
They urged both camps to agree that Protestants could march through the Catholic zone one year but would not do so the following year.
"It is not a settlement but it would create the breathing space both sides need, leaving the way clear for confidence-building and discussions, leading to a lasting settlement," the papers said.
A senior Orange Order official dismissed the idea.
"The suggestion about the two-year plan is something that I think is not really very feasible," executive officer George Patton told BBC radio.
He said the papers had not recognised that the Order had made concessions by reducing the number of marches in the Portadown area from 10 previously to one now.
Two Catholics were killed and many police and civilians were injured when rioting swept the region last July.

Protestants blocked roads and rioted when police banned the Orange Order from marching through a Catholic part of Portadown. Catholic violence flared in several towns when the police later reversed the ban.
Hostilities between extremist groups and anxiety about the annual "marching season" have clouded hopes of an early political settlement in the province.
The Irish Republican Army, which has waged a 28-year war to end British rule, has rejected calls for an end to violence.
Loyalist militia, who support continued rule from London, have killed two nationalists in recent revenge attacks.
